entries.title: Cook County judge rejects push to appoint special prosecutor to probe Chicago area deportation blitz
entries.summary: <p>A judge on Thursday refused to install a special prosecutor in the Cook County state’s attorney’s office to probe alleged crimes stemming from the Operation Midway Blitz deportation campaign last year.</p><p>During a hearing at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse, Cook County Circuit Court Judge Erica Reddick flatly rejected the arguments of a broad coalition that sought a special prosecutor to target the federal agents who carried out the immigration enforcement effort, which led to two shootings and rocked Chicago and the surrounding suburbs for months.</p><p>The coalition of elected officials, clergy, journalists and attorneys had argued that Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke had turned a “blind eye” to “egregious acts of violence” by the federal agents, and that O’Neill Burke’s close working relationship with the feds amounted to a conflict of interest.</p><p>Reddick’s ruling amounts to a major victory for O’Neill Burke, who had fought the petition to appoint a special prosecutor and argued that such a move could actually hinder efforts to prosecute crimes tied to Midway Blitz.</p><p>Calls for the investigation and prosecution of federal agents <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/02/06/how-can-chicagos-top-prosecutor-hold-ice-accountable" target="_blank" ><u>intensified early this year</u></a>, following the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by immigration authorities in Minneapolis.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/05/ice-midway-blitz-chicago-trump-silverio-villegas-gonzalez" >Illinois State Police investigating deadly ICE shooting of Silverio Villegas González in Chicago suburb</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The October shooting in Chicago of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" ><u>Marimar Martinez</u></a> by a Border Patrol agent prompted a federal<b> </b>investigation, according to her attorney. But it wasn't until late April that the Illinois State Police <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/05/ice-midway-blitz-chicago-trump-silverio-villegas-gonzalez" target="_blank" ><u>began investigating</u></a> the September killing of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/15/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-fatally-shot-by-ice-agents-touched-the-lives-of-so-many-loved-ones-say" target="_blank" ><u>Silverio</u><b><u> </u></b><u>Villegas</u><b><u> </u></b><u>González</u></a><b> </b>by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Franklin Park.</p><p>The Illinois State Police investigation began at the request of Franklin Park police. O'Neill Burke's office has promised to play a "supportive role"<b> </b>in the probe.</p><p>The group behind the special prosecutor push filed its petition March 12. The coalition includes U.S. Reps. Jesus “Chuy”<b> </b>Garcia, Jonathan<b> </b>Jackson<b> </b>and Delia Ramirez, all Democrats; and former U.S. District Chief Judge Ruben Castillo, who was appointed to the bench in 1994<b> </b>by President Bill Clinton.</p><p>It also includes the Chicago News Guild, which represents journalists at the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>In addition to the shootings of Martinez and González, the group has pointed to batteries, assaults, kidnappings and other violence, all allegedly at the hands of federal agents.</p><p>Castillo led a separate group, known as the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/04/30/pritzker-illinois-accountability-commission-operation-midway-blitz-trump-immigration" target="_blank" ><u>Illinois Accountability Commission</u></a>, that last month accused the agents of regularly using force against Illinois residents “without justification.” The commission, formed by Gov. JB Pritzker, referred its findings to O’Neill Burke along with other prosecutors and police departments. Its work seemed to trigger the recent investigation<b> </b>into González's death.</p><p>“I would say to State’s Attorney Burke, that if she doesn’t want to investigate, step aside,” Castillo said. “Step aside. And let a special prosecutor come in and do what needs to be done. But someone needs to do it.”</p><p>O’Neill Burke insisted her office can only bring charges “after receiving a completed investigation from a law enforcement agency.”</p><p>Prosecuting federal agents in state court would require showing that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/01/08/can-state-officials-prosecute-the-feds-calls-grow-after-minneapolis-shooting" target="_blank" ><u>they acted unreasonably</u></a> while fulfilling their duties. Prosecutors like O’Neill Burke have discretion to choose which cases they pursue,<b> </b>and she released guidance outlining her approach<b> </b>in February.</p><p>Under the plan, a law enforcement agency would lead a criminal investigation by collecting and preserving evidence. Then, prosecutors would conduct an independent review of all evidence and make charging decisions.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/24/chicago-trump-midway-blitz-crime-ice-border-patrol-oneill-burke" >Ruling on whether to appoint a special prosecutor to probe Midway Blitz agents expected in coming weeks</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>But weeks later, the coalition filed a petition that accused O’Neill Burke of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-cook-county-oneill-burke-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor" target="_blank" ><u>turning a “blind eye”</u></a> to “egregious acts of violence”<b> </b>by Midway Blitz agents.<b> </b>The coalition complained that she’d “never stated publicly that she has any intention to investigate these crimes,” and it suggested she might fear White House retaliation.</p><p>O’Neill Burke countered that she’s not intimidated by “vague”<b> </b>threats of political retaliation. She called the coalition’s efforts “frivolous”<b> </b>and<b> </b>“heavy-handed”<b> </b>and said it <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/24/chicago-cook-county-trump-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor-oneill-burke-loevy" target="_blank" ><u>could actually “thwart” justice</u></a>.</p><p>Then the coalition <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/21/oneill-burke-trump-midway-blitz-special-prosecutor-chicago-cook-county" target="_blank" ><u>pointed to emails</u></a> sent last August, when President Donald Trump<b> </b>threatened to deploy National Guard troops into Chicago. O’Neill Burke’s office declined to sign on to a statement criticizing the Trump administration because she wanted to maintain her “excellent working relationships”<b> </b>with federal law enforcement.</p><p>“The State’s Attorney has an alliance with federal law enforcement that prevents her from taking action against the federal agents alleged to have committed crimes during Operation Midway Blitz,” the coalition’s<b> </b>lawyers wrote.</p><p><i>Neither the reporter nor editors who worked on this story — including some represented by the News Guild — have been involved in the litigation described in this article.</i></p>

entries.title: 'I will get justice' — Chicago man vs. the government of Saudi Arabia
entries.summary: <p>Ahmed Abdul Majeed wants justice.</p><p>Born in India, for more than 40 years he lived in Saudi Arabia, employed at a travel agency, booking trips for the royal family, building the company.</p><p>"I used to work a lot," he said. "Seven days a week."</p><p>For the past two years, Majeed, 67, has lived in the Devon Avenue Indian community with his son, Ahmed Abdulumer, a food delivery driver and American citizen. It was his son, 34, who brought Majeed to my attention.</p><p>"My father," Abdulumer wrote, "was a victim of forced labor and human trafficking."</p><p>The details are complicated. We should probably start by explaining the kafala system, the tradition of immigrants existing in rightless limbo in Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern nations.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-aa0000" name="module-aa0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>"Unfortunately, migrant workers in Saudi Arabia have little to no control over their lives," Abdulumer wrote. "The status quo in Saudi Arabia for decades has been the kafala system for migrant workers which had been exploiting, stealing wages, imprisoning, raping, falsifying charges and killing countless workers over many decades. This system strips workers of their freedom and dignity, silences complaints and grants employers near-total control over their lives."</p> <p>Some workers are brought in under false pretenses. Others enter with eyes open — the money is good, relative to their homelands. Being on the bottom of the social ladder in Saudi Arabia is still better than being on the bottom of the social ladder in Bangladesh.</p><p>Majeed put in four decades in an office, only to be threatened with arrest, his passport seized, then forced to work for free for six months, sell the family home in India and hand over the proceeds — about $100,000 — to get his passport back and be allowed to leave the country.</p><p>Given the notoriously brutal conditions foreign workers face, what did Majeed expect would happen?</p><p>"I'm supposed to have a good life with my family after serving the four decades," he said. "We built a company from scratch. I never expected the person who generated millions of dollars to the company end up selling his own property."</p><p>From the moment he left Saudi Arabia, Majeed has been trying to get satisfaction for how he was treated.</p><p>"I landed in India 8th of September, 2020," he said. "Immediately I went to the prime minister's office. I traveled by train with my son" — he has four children. "We tried to meet the prime minister of India. He did not meet me, but he forwarded my case to the Indian embassy in Riyadh. No response."</p><p>How many survivors of kafala system abuses are in Chicago? Numbers are impossible to find. The Indian consulate said they know nothing about it. </p><p>"No one from the Indian diaspora mentioned or complained of any such thing as yet," said Sanjeev Kumar Pal, the press officer at the Consulate General of India in Chicago.</p><p>Organizations that keep track of immigrant workers rights sometimes encounter similar situations.</p><p>"We're grateful it's not something super common," said Shelly Ruzicka, communications director at Arise Chicago, a West Side group that helps immigrant workers recover stolen wages. "We have some stories, particularly with au pairs, sometimes with the J-1 visa."</p><p>She was referring to problems in this country, not Saudi Arabia. With the rise of ICE, and immigrants being demonized and shorn of legal protections, the threat of the United States ending up with its own de facto kafala system is a real possibility.</p><p>"Yes," agreed Ruzicka. "We are very worried about that, under this administration. We're starting to hear stories. We're seeing a dilution of [immigrant workers'] rights. They are made to be more fearful, reluctant to speak up. Immigrant workers' bosses are feeling bolder. Different types of abuses are fairly common in low paid jobs — regular injuries on high speed machines, not being paid overtime, things like that we are seeing on a regular basis."</p><p>Majeed is clawing at a brick wall. What keeps him going?</p><p>"The day I landed here, I decided to fight for justice, he said. "There are so many people like my case. The Saudis have to realize: you cannot deny justice for the people who serve you. The world must know."</p><p>After years of effort, he's had "zero response." So how is a story in the Sun-Times going to help?</p><p>"Once it is published in the Sun-Times, I am sure Saudi embassy will take note and they will contact me and I will get justice before I pass this world," Majeed said. "I am sure about this."</p><p>And if nothing happens? Will he ever give up?</p><p>"I cannot," he said. "But I am sure, a newspaper like yours, which millions of people read, the Saudi embassy will take note. They will contact me. And I will get justice."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/08/deportation-francisco-gonzalez-jasso-panchito-gang-latin-kings-deported-ice-mexico-midway-blitz-little-village" >Labeled a gang member and deported, longtime Chicagoan tries to restart in his Mexican hometown</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/02/a-chicago-couple-separated-by-midway-blitz-is-determined-to-reunite" >A Chicago couple separated by Midway Blitz is determined to reunite</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

>Microplastics found in Lake Michigan, Chicago River, other Illinois waterways</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whrlriy-l-z/" target="_blank" >Brett Chase</a></h5><p><b>Tiny big problem?</b>: Test samplings of Lake Michigan, the Chicago River and other waterways across Illinois found tiny plastics were present, posing potential threats to human health and damage to the environment, according to an advocacy group.</p><p><b>What was found</b>: In all, 31 test sites, including multiple samplings along Lake Michigan, showed broken-down plastics in the water. Known as microplastics, these small particles are being studied by government and academic researchers for possible links to illnesses including cancer. Plastics don’t easily break down in the environment and also threaten fish and wildlife.</p><p><b>At issue</b>: Plastic food containers and bags, clothing fibers, pellets used in manufacturing, and many other sources contribute to water pollution, according to the report released Thursday by Environment Illinois Research and Education Center. Single-use plastics, "fast fashion" trends and stormwater runoff from factories using plastic pellets are among the biggest sources of water contamination, the report says.</p><p><a class="Link" entries.title: Fundraiser launched for high school basketball captain killed in West Side double murder with Uber driver
entries.summary: <p>A fundraiser has been launched for 18-year-old high school basketball captain Damarion Johnson, who was shot and killed in an East Garfield Park double murder earlier this month along with his Uber driver.</p><p>Candace Johnson launched the <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/support-for-damarions-funeral-and-family-needs" target="_blank" >fundraiser</a> earlier this month, calling her son's loss "an unimaginable pain in our hearts." </p><p>"No mother should have to bury her child, and asking for help is not easy," Johnson said through the fundraiser. "Your kindness and support will help lighten the burden during one of the darkest moments of our lives."</p><p>As of Thursday afternoon, over $1,800 of the family's $9,000 goal has been raised. </p><p>Damarion Johnson and Jassen Cho, who was driving for Uber at the time of the shooting, were driving in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/08/high-school-senior-and-man-38-gunned-down-in-garfield-park-neighborhood" target="_blank" >200 block of North Homan Avenue</a> around 8:30 p.m. May 7 when someone inside a gray SUV fired at them, Chicago police said.</p><p>A Hyundai Tucson linked to the shooting was soon found blocks away, according to a police report obtained by the Sun-Times. It had been set ablaze.</p><p>Cho was pronounced dead at Mount Sinai Hospital at 8:54 p.m., while Johnson died at 8:57 p.m. at Stroger Hospital, both from multiple gunshot wounds, according to the Cook County medical examiner’s office, which ruled their deaths homicides.</p><p>A person of interest in the slayings, a 17-year-old boy, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/14/person-of-interest-arrested-in-west-side-slayings-of-uber-driver-high-school-basketball-player-source" target="_blank" >was arrested and then released </a>without being charged about a week after the attack. </p><p>"As a mother of 8 children, I am now trying to navigate this tragedy while continuing to care for my other 7 children who are also devastated by the loss of their brother," Johnson wrote. <br></p>

entries.title: Incendio sospechoso en casa de West Englewood deja a 2 menores muertos y a 4 personas en estado grave
entries.summary: <p>Una niña de 8 años y un joven de 15 años murieron tras un incendio de alarma adicional ocurrido temprano el miércoles en el vecindario de West Englewood, y otros cuatro quedaron en estado grave, informaron las autoridades.</p><p>La policía está investigando el incendio como un caso de incendio intencional.</p><p>La niña de 8 años fue declarada muerta a las 2:57 a.m.; el adolescente de 15 años, a las 2:49 a.m., según la Oficina del Médico Forense del Condado de Cook. Sus nombres no han sido divulgados.</p><p>El concejal Raymond Lopez (15.º), quien habló con los reporteros en el lugar, calificó el incendio de "intencional" y la policía anunció el miércoles por la tarde una investigación por incendio provocado. </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-240000" name="module-240000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Se encontró un dispositivo incendiario, según fuentes.</p><p>Parece que el fuego se originó desde el exterior de la casa y posiblemente fue el resultado de una discusión entre vecinos, dijo López. No dio más detalles.</p><p>El incendio se desató alrededor de la 1:50 a.m. en la cuadra 6200 al sur de Paulina Street. Casi 200 miembros del Departamento de Bomberos de Chicago (CFD) respondieron, según informaron.</p><p>Seis personas fueron rescatadas de la casa y trasladadas a hospitales cercanos. Todos estaban inicialmente en estado grave, según CFD.</p><p>Un vecino que pidió no ser identificado le dijo al Chicago Sun-Times que una mujer vivía en la casa con varios niños, algunos adolescentes y “otros pequeños”. La mujer había vivido en la casa durante aproximadamente cuatro años, dijo el vecino, quien agregó que a veces veía a hombres sentados en el porche.</p><p>"Si esto es en realidad un incendio provocado, necesitamos atrapar y llevar a la justicia a los responsables de este acto", destacó López. "Ninguna cantidad de desacuerdo o animosidad da a nadie licencia para incendiar la casa de alguien a media noche, y mucho menos cuando hay niños presentes".</p><p>Un vecino vio el fuego y llamó al 911, agregó López. La rápida respuesta del CFD probablemente evitó que el incendio se propagara más por la calle, agregó.</p><p>"En este momento, no conocemos la naturaleza exacta de la causa", dijo López. "Pero sabemos que, a diferencia de los incendios que a veces se ven en casas abandonadas, donde inician incendios para calentarse, ese no parece ser este el caso", dijo López.</p><p>El concejal está pidiendo a los residentes que proporcionen cualquier grabación de video que pueda ser útil.</p><p>"Esta casa estaba ocupada. Esta casa tenía niños en su interior. Esta casa fue incendiada, por lo que voy a hacer un llamado a toda la comunidad para que revisen sus cámaras Ring, cualquier cámara que tengan en sus hogares, entre la medianoche y la 1:30 a.m.".</p><p>West Englewood es una "gran comunidad con muchos niños", destacó López. "Estoy seguro de que los padres de todo el vecindario van a abrazar a sus hijos un poco más fuerte hoy".</p><p>Para ayudar a los heridos en el incendio, contacta a la oficina de López en ward15@cityofchicago.org o al 773-823-1539.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: 'Broadview Six' case will be dropped after closed-door hearing about grand jury transcripts
entries.summary: <p>Charges against the remaining members of the "Broadview Six" will be permanently dropped following a closed-door hearing Thursday morning about redactions that were made by prosecutors to a set of grand jury transcripts.</p><p>U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros made the announcement just hours after the hearing, as prosecutors and defense attorneys reconvened in U.S. District Judge April Perry's courtroom at the Dirksen Federal Courthouse. </p><p>It puts an end to one of the most contentious cases brought during Operation Midway Blitz, the deportation campaign that rocked the Chicago area last fall.</p><p>Perry had called off the trial, set to begin next week, following the hearing earlier Thursday. She announced that news after speaking privately with the lawyers in the case for about 50 minutes. Court staff let members of the public and media back into Perry's courtroom before she shared the update. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/29/broadview-ice-crime-chicago-trump-kat-abughezaleh" >Feds drop conspiracy charge against ‘Broadview Six’ ICE protesters, who still face trial for impeding officer</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The Chicago Sun-Times, WBEZ, the Chicago Tribune and the Better Government Association <a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/9e/77/205924394d06bfa2059e43dedf19/rabbittintervene.pdf" target="_blank" >intervened in the case</a> Thursday morning, arguing the hearing should take place on the public record. Perry heard from media lawyer Steven Mandell but said, "the interest in guaranteeing a fair jury to these defendants is more compelling than allowing access to this particular proceeding."</p><p>Perry then cleared the courtroom, and court security roped off the area of the hallway nearby for the duration of the closed-door session.</p><p>The case is one of the most highly publicized prosecutions to result from Operation Midway Blitz deportation campaign. That’s because it <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/29/kat-abughazaleh-conspiracy-indictment-broadview-protests-donald-trump-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" ><u>began as a conspiracy case</u></a> against six people who protested outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in suburban Broadview.</p><p>But the feds <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" ><u>dropped charges against two</u></a> of the original six, and then they <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/29/broadview-ice-crime-chicago-trump-kat-abughezaleh" target="_blank" ><u>abandoned the conspiracy charge</u></a> altogether. Now, four people face one misdemeanor count each of forcibly impeding a federal agent.</p><p>Charged are former congressional candidate Kat Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt and Andre Martin, who served as a member of Abughazaleh’s campaign staff.</p><p>The latest charging document in the case, filed April 29, does not offer specific allegations against the defendants. But they’ve generally been accused of joining a larger group of protesters who surrounded an ICE agent’s vehicle and pushed, scratched and otherwise damaged it as it approached the facility in Broadview.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/04/broadview-six-grand-jury-transcript-conspiracy" target="_blank" >Remaining ‘Broadview Six’ defendants move to disclose grand jury transcripts, drop conspiracy charges</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>With trial nearing Tuesday, controversy over a set of transcripts from grand jury proceedings seemed to put the case on the rocks. Defense attorneys sought access to transcripts showing how the conspiracy law had been explained to grand jurors.</p><p>Judge Perry agreed to look at them on her own.</p><p>Grand jury proceedings are generally treated with secrecy, with panels hearing only from prosecutors and their witnesses before deciding whether to hand up an indictment.</p><p>Prosecutors wound up redacting portions of the transcripts they gave Perry. She asked them to bring unredacted copies to an April 29 hearing. But moments into it, prosecutors announced they’d be dismissing the conspiracy charge and abandoning the grand jury’s indictment — proceeding with misdemeanor charges in a separate charging document.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/18/broadview-6-ice-midway-blitz-trump-deportation-kat-abughazaleh" >Trial nearing in case of remaining ‘Broadview 6' ICE protesters, who may be labeled members of a ‘mob’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Defense attorneys continued to push for their disclosure anyway. Straw attorney Christopher Parente urged Perry during a hearing Monday simply to look at an unredacted version, arguing that prosecutors may be hiding something that “could have tainted all of this.”</p><p>Prosecutors said they had no objection, so Perry agreed to take a look.<b> </b>She seemed skeptical at the time, though, telling them “if I had to guess, it seemed like those were probably related to IT issues.”</p><p>Two days later, the judge demanded the appearance in her courtroom of “any”<b> </b>prosecutor “who participated in the decision to redact portions”<b> </b>of the transcript, “whether on the trial team or at the supervisory level.”</p><p>Perry said she’d hold the hearing under seal to avoid tainting the jury pool, and because grand jury matters would be discussed.</p>

entries.title: Colson Montgomery standing tall at shortstop for White Sox
entries.summary: <p>A question around Colson Montgomery as he progressed through the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a>’ system was whether he could stay at shortstop. Nobody was wondering about the former high school basketball star’s athleticism, but a look at Montgomery’s lanky 6-3 frame indicated that a move to a corner infield spot or the outfield was possible.</p><p>Montgomery has played 102 big-league games at short, and he makes it clear that he wants to stay at the position.</p><p>“It’s how you play,” Montgomery said. “If you prove and show you can make the outs, you can keep your range, and things like that, why can’t you stay there? That kind of keeps my mindset focused on I’m a shortstop and that’s where I want to play.”</p><p>A year into his Sox career, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/29/erick-fedde-white-sox-angels" >Montgomery</a> has shown he can play short at a major-league level. After compiling six outs above average at shortstop in only 60 games last year, Montgomery is off to a strong start in 2026. He’s already matched the six outs above average and sits third in baseball, behind only the Royals’ Bobby Witt Jr. (13) and the Brewers’ Joey Ortiz (7).</p><p>Numbers aside, Montgomery’s quick-twitch skills and feel for the position have stood out. Sox manager Will Venable has been impressed with Montgomery’s consistency, whether it’s making the average play, showing range to either side or charging in on a slow grounder and making a bare-handed grab.</p><p>“A lot of it for some of these guys is just making the routine play and he has just been incredibly consistent in making the plays he should,” Venable said. “And then he’s able to tap into the athleticism and make some special plays as well.”</p><p>The inquiry comes up because, historically, shortstops haven’t stood as tall as Montgomery. The reasons are somewhat obvious: shorter players are believed to have a lower center of gravity, allowing for increased quickness, a better range of motion and closeness to the ground to pick up ground balls.</p><p>On Opening Day this year, the average height of the 29 starting shortstops other than Montgomery was 72.2 inches, or just a tick above 6 feet. Though it’s an imperfect metric, Gold Glove shortstops since 2021 have averaged 72.1 inches. Only 2021 American League winner Carlos Correa (6-3) is listed as tall as Montgomery.</p><p>But that doesn’t mean a good shortstop has to be 6 feet. The position has trended taller, and athleticism and solid positioning are more important than proximity to the ground.</p><p>Before he was hired by the Sox, Venable spent two seasons with the Rangers as associate manager on Bruce Bochy’s staff. Venable picked up a World Series ring when Texas won the 2023 World Series, and that Rangers team was fueled by 6-4 shortstop Corey Seager.</p><p>Last year, Seager put up a career-high 16 defensive runs saved above average, and has finished in the top 5 of his league five times in range factor per game among shortstops. Seager has also played shortstop for two championship teams: those Rangers and the 2020 Dodgers.</p><p>“To me, if you can play your position, you can play your position,” Venable said. “Being around Corey Seager, he does a fine job of it. I get it, but if guys can make plays, they can make plays.”</p><p>Montgomery is focusing on doing that for the Sox. Though his power is eye-catching, he said he takes the most pride in his defense because of the earlier questions about his size.</p><p>“I come in every single day, do whatever I can to get my body and my mind ready to play the best nine innings of defense that I can,” Montgomery said.</p>

entries.title: S.L. Price goes deep into lacrosse, Northwestern with book 'The American Game'
entries.summary: <p>To S.L. Price, the emergence of Northwestern’s women’s lacrosse team as a national power can’t be overstated.</p><p>“I think it’s the most unlikely build in American sports history,” he said.</p><p>Price knows a thing or two about sports, having spent 26 years at Sports Illustrated and becoming one of the best sportswriters in the industry. His most recent book, “The American Game: History and Hope in the Country of Lacrosse,” includes the rise of Northwestern, which will host the NCAA women’s championship this weekend at Martin Stadium.</p><p>It will mark the first time that the championship will be played outside of the Eastern Time Zone. Top-seeded Northwestern will face No. 4 Johns Hopkins in the second semifinal at 4:30 p.m. Friday on ESPNU. The winner will face either No. 3 Maryland or No. 2 North Carolina at 11 a.m. Sunday on ESPN.</p><p>As part of his examination of the history of lacrosse — which Price calls America’s original sport, invented by the Iroquois, now called the Haudenosaunee, a thousand years ago — Price explains how coach Kelly Amonte Hiller, starting at age 26, built the Northwestern program from nothing, literally pulling players off the street.</p><p>“Her foundation where the Koester twins, Ashley and Courtney, who weren’t lacrosse players,” Price said. “In 2001, she saw them dodging around in a touch-football game, and then she sees them jogging. Finally, she runs out and says, ‘Excuse me, do you know what lacrosse is?’ And they had no idea. She gives them a couple sticks, and that’s the foundation.”</p><p>Hiller has led NU to eight national championships. But after winning seven from 2005 to ’12, Northwestern didn’t win again until 2023. Price said that during that gap, Hiller reevaluated her coaching style. She learned to lower the pressure on her players, and it eventually led to another title.</p><p>“So she caught the world unawares, the world caught up with her and then she adjusted,” Price said. “That’s a real sign of a great coach.”</p><p>Price spent six years reporting for the 560-page book, which was nominated for a 2026 Dan Jenkins Medal for Excellence in Sportswriting. Though he was never “a lacrosse guy,” the topic was in his wheelhouse, where sports intersect with culture.</p><p>“It’s just a unique, fascinating subculture that I think mirrors American culture like almost nothing else does,” he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-310000" entries.title: Festival Sueños regresa a Grant Park con Fuerza Regida y una gran variedad de vendedores de comida
entries.summary: <p>Para Liana Lorenzo y su familia, asistir al Festival de Música Sueños en Grant Park se ha convertido en una tradición anual.</p><p>Con más de una docena de miembros de la familia de 21 a 45 años, la familia de Lorenzo es una de las muchas familias multigeneracionales que esperan con ansias el festival de dos días durante el fin de semana del Día de los Caídos. La programación de este año incluye a J Balvin, Kali Uchis, Danny Ocean, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/11/19/festival-suenos-2026-anuncia-su-primer-artista-principal-fuerza-regida" target="_blank" >Fuerza Regida</a>, Yandel y Ryan Castro.</p><p>"La música realmente nos une", dijo Lorenzo. "Ahora somos mayores y podemos coordinar nuestros horarios un poco mejor. Sueños es algo que esperamos como grupo porque todos sabemos, a pesar de nuestros horarios locos, que nos reunimos para esto".</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e00000" name="module-e00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El festival se lleva a cabo tras un año difícil para la comunidad latina de Chicago. Desde el Operativo Midway Blitz el otoño pasado, la campaña de deportación de la administración de Trump ha mantenido a la comunidad en tensión.</p><p>Pero durante el fin de semana de Sueños, los asistentes esperan celebrar la comida, el idioma y la cultura latina juntos. Esos momentos se sienten "alegres", dijo Franea Arceo, propietaria de El Taconazo Express junto con su papá, Eduardo. Su restaurante ha operado un puesto en Sueños desde 2023.</p><p>Arceo dijo que el festival no ha comunicado a los vendedores de comida cómo podría responder si agentes del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) aparecen en o alrededor de Grant Park durante el festival, pero ella y sus empleados generalmente se sienten seguros durante el evento de dos días.</p><p>"Vamos sabiendo que estamos asumiendo un riesgo", agregó Arceo. "[Pero] también tenemos que trabajar y proveer para nuestras familias".</p><p>Lorenzo dijo que Sueños es un fin de semana para que las familias se reconecten entre todas las demás cosas que suceden en el mundo.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-070abe" name="image-070abe"></a> <picture Vístete en capas que te puedas quitar, lleva una chaqueta o suéter para después del atardecer, y lleva un pequeño poncho plegable en tu bolso por si llueve.</p><p>"Somos una familia que pasa tiempo junta constantemente, así que esto es solo otra cosa que añadimos a la lista", dijo Vanessa Valdés, una prima de Lorenzo. Valdés desearía que la programación musical de este año fuera más sólida, pero dijo que el verdadero foco es pasar el fin de semana juntos. "Siempre lo hacemos divertido".</p><p>Otra prima, Evette Lorenzo, dijo que Sueños la lleva a un lugar nostálgico.</p><p>"Era casi como si fuéramos niños de nuevo. Estábamos gritando, sólo actuando como tontos. Estoy contenta de que aún podamos hacer eso", agregó Evette.</p><p>Aquí hay otros consejos para el fin de semana —desde actos musicales hasta comida— según los asiduos al festival.</p><p></p><h3><b>Lo que no te puedes perder </b></h3><p>Quien encabeza el programa es José Álvaro Osorio Balvín, conocido simplemente como J Balvin, que regresa a Sueños el sábado.</p><p>Balvín hizo historia en Grant Park al convertirse en el primer latino en ser el acto principal de Lollapalooza en 2019. Unos años más tarde, en 2022, regresó a Chicago con un electrizante set del líder del programa, en el que presentó sus clásicas canciones "Mi Gente", "Ginza" y "Loco contigo".</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-4b1631" name="image-4b1631"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/462f20e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5363x3010+0+536/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe0%2F13%2Fa811e0eb4de8bb6dc99886fce313%2Fsuenos-fest-052922-26.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/68fc347/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5363x3010+0+536/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe0%2F13%2Fa811e0eb4de8bb6dc99886fce313%2Fsuenos-fest-052922-26.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3ae0df1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5363x3010+0+536/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe0%2F13%2Fa811e0eb4de8bb6dc99886fce313%2Fsuenos-fest-052922-26.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="El concierto de J. Evette y su hermana disfrutaron de su set mientras mezclaba la música house y freestyle de Chicago con música en español, dijo ella. Las hermanas vieron cómo la multitud creció de unas 20 personas a unas 200.</p><p>"Si no hubiera sido por caminar y aventurarnos más allá del escenario principal, lo habríamos perdido por completo. Fue simplemente muy divertido", dijo Evette.</p><p>Artistas locales que harán apariciones en Sueños incluyen a <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/vanguardiachi/" target="_blank" >Grupo Vanguardia</a> y Los de la Homan, dos grupos regional mexicano en ascenso, además de los DJs <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/5/17/23066990/suenos-music-chicago-grant-park-jd-miriam-reggaeton-dj-balvin" target="_blank" >Miriam</a> y <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/djchavaa/?hl=en" target="_blank" >Chava</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/lemanz.oficial/?hl=en" target="_blank" >LEMANZ</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/bompleneras/" target="_blank" >Las Bompleneras</a> y muchos más.</p><p>También habrá una clase de bachata que se llevará a cabo en el escenario de La Plaza el sábado por la tarde y una clase de salsa al mismo tiempo el domingo.</p><p></p><h3><b>El sabor local </b></h3><p>No es un secreto que Chicago es una de las mejores ciudades gastronómicas del mundo. Gran parte de eso se debe a las contribuciones de inmigrantes latinoamericanos que operan cientos de restaurantes, bares y carritos de comida en toda la ciudad y no hay escasez de ellos en Sueños.</p><p>La sección de La Plaza del festival albergará alrededor de dos docenas de vendedores. Prueba los diferentes sabores de empanadas al estilo argentino en <a class="Link" href="https://5411empanadas.com/" target="_blank" >5411 Empanadas</a>, clásicos colombianos en <a class="Link" href="https://www.arepageorge.com/" target="_blank" >ArePA George</a>, o carnitas de <a class="Link" href="https://carnitasoriginaldonalfredo.com/" target="_blank" >Carnitas Don Alfredo</a>.</p><p>El <a class="Link" href="https://poncerestaurant.com/" target="_blank" >Restaurante Ponce</a> del vecindario de Belmont Cragin es un favorito familiar para Lorenzo y sus primos. “Definitivamente pidan target="_blank" >n</a> en su puesto en el festival para disfrutar de una de las mejores comidas mexicanas de Chicago, con tacos, burritos y birria.</p><p>En el puesto de comida El Taconazo Express, Arceo y su equipo esperan servir cientos de tacos durante el ajetreado fin de semana.</p><p>¿En el menú? Carne asada, al pastor, lengua y barbacoa. También se han sumado a la tendencia de la quesabirria y la incluirán en su menú del festival.</p><p>Pero si no tienes antojo de comida latina, hay algo para todos. Puedes conseguir un clásico sándwich Italian Beef al estilo Chicago en Frannie’s Beef o disfrutar de unas costillas de BBQ de <a class="Link" href="https://rib1.com/" target="_blank" >Robinson’s No. 1 Ribs</a>.</p><p>Los asistentes con entradas de admisión general pueden disfrutar de hamburguesas y papas fritas de Bust Outs, auténtica comida mexicana de <a class="Link" href="https://sabrosochicago.com/" target="_blank" >Sabroso! Mexican Grill</a>, tacos de pescado al estilo Baja de <a class="Link" href="https://donpezfishtacos.com/" target="_blank" >Don Pez</a> y clásicos puertorriqueños de <a class="Link" href="https://orderlabombatogo.com/" target="_blank" >La Bomba</a>.</p><p></p><h3><b>Evaluando el quinto aniversario </b></h3><p>El Festival Sueños se presenta como el festival de música latina más grande del Medio Oeste.</p><p>Fue fundado por los creadores del Baja Beach Fest de México, Aarón Ampudia y Chris Den Ujil, a través de su empresa La Cultura Presenta LLC. Han producido y dirigido Sueños cada año en colaboración con los productores de Lollapalooza C3 Presents (<a class="Link" href="https://www.billboard.com/music/music-news/live-nation-completes-deal-for-c3-presents-6414053/" target="_blank" >adquirida por Live Nation en 2014</a>) y Reventón Promotions.</p><p>Aunque el primer año se promocionó como un festival de reggaetón, Sueños se ha expandido para incluir más actos de música regional mexicana, como los populares Grupo Frontera y Grupo Firme.</p><p>Los organizadores obtuvieronun <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2024/07/11/los-organizadores-del-suenos-music-festival-llegan-a-un-acuerdo-de-cinco-anos-con-el-distrito-de-parques-de-chicago" target="_blank" >acuerdo de cinco años con el Distrito de Parques de Chicago</a> en 2024, lo que asegura que el festival continuará como un elemento básico de Grant Park al menos hasta 2029. El acuerdo incluye la opción de una extensión de cinco años y una asistencia pagada limitada a 75,000 personas por día. También especifica que los organizadores deben reparar y restaurar los terrenos del parque una vez que el evento haya terminado.</p><p>El Distrito de Parques recibirá un pago garantizado de $1.5 millones o de $15 a $19 por entrada, dependiendo de cuál sea mayor, por el festival de dos días. El acuerdo incluye la posibilidad de ampliar el festival a tres días, aunque aún no se ha concretado.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: Bears focused on what they've got after failing to add help at D-end
entries.summary: <p>Edge rushers Joey Bosa, Jadeveon Clowney, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/05/09/cam-jordan-bears-cameron-dc-dennis-allen-not-much-conversation-about-pass-rush-defensive-end" target="_blank" >Cam Jordan</a> and Von Miller have a whopping 24 Pro Bowl appearances to their names. They’re also quite available, having yet to sign with any NFL team in free agency.</p><p>After an offseason in which the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> did little to solve their pass-rush problem, adding no free agents or draft picks of consequence, it’s tempting to wonder what they, or any other available defensive ends, would look like with a wishbone C on their helmet.</p><p>“I can't focus on it,” Bears defensive line coach Jeremy Garrett said Thursday. “My focus is on, 'This is who we have in the building. How can I get these guys better?’... I don't focus on the names and the theories. I can't do that."</p><p>They’re household names. Three of the four were drafted in the top three overall. Two have played for Bears defensive coordinator Dennis Allen at previous stops. But all of them are in their 30s, are likely limited to niche pass rush roles and used to making premium paychecks — which explains why they remain available.</p><p>The Bears continue to monitor edge rushers in free agency or those who might be available via trade. The fact remains, though, that they won’t be able to find any long-term answer until next offseason at the earliest. That’s concerning, given how troublesome the team’s pass rush was last season, when six teams had fewer defensive pressures and only one had a worse pass-rush win rate.</p><p>The Bears' takeaways masked their pass-rush struggles, but only to a point. The Bears defense led the NFL in interceptions with 23 last year. There have been 55 teams since 2000 with at least 23 interceptions in a season — and only 12 of those teams had fewer sacks than the Bears’ 35. Since Pro Football Reference began tracking defensive pressures in 2018, only one team has posted fewer of them while intercepting at least 20 passes in a season.</p><p>The Bears’ only remaining path is to try to improve their core four defensive ends — Montez Sweat, Austin Booker, Dayo Odeyingbo and Shemar Turner.</p><p>Last month, head coach Ben Johnson said the Bears’ edge rush improvement would be tied to the “combination of us being able to coach better and those guys taking the next step.” Garrett said he’s focused his edge rushers on three goals: to force more tackles for loss on run plays to set up longer passing downs; to be more consistent in their pass rush technique; and to find a way to affect the quarterback.</p><p>“When you watch tape from last year, there’s some meat on the bone,” Garrett said.</p><p>Odeyingbo had only one sack in eight games last year before tearing his Achilles’ tendon. Turner had none in five games before tearing his ACL. The Bears envision both being able to play end on first and second down before moving inside to rush the passer on third downs.</p><p>Sweat, who turns 30 in September, posted 10 sacks last season — less than half that of Myles Garrett, who led the league with 23. Austin Booker had 4½ in 10 games.</p><p>Two weeks ago, defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said that he focused too much on scheme and too little on fundamentals last year. To that end, the Bears’ defensive line room didn’t talk about scheme for the first two weeks of the offseason program, focusing only on individual skills like get-off, hand placement and leverage. Garrett has never been part of a team that did that before.</p><p>“It's been really good for our guys,” he said, “and really good for our room.”</p><p>The better question, though, is whether that will be good enough.</p><p><b>NOTE</b>: The Bears waived running back Deion Hankins and replaced him with Salvon Ahmed, who had 163 career carries with the Dolphins under new Bears position coach Eric Studesville. The Bears also signed safety Anthony Johnson Jr. and put Aussie punter Tory Taylor on the exempt/international player list, where can remain until the Bears release their 53-man roster.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Tim O'Malley, actor who danced, joked and sang about addiction on stage in 'Godshow,' dies at 68
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Tim O'Malley, a comic actor who unflinchingly told his story of overcoming addiction in "Godshow," died May 11 from natural causes at his Beverly home. He was 68.</p><p>In a 2003 Sun-Times story following its debut, Mr. O'Malley spoke at length about the show and people's reaction to it.</p><p>"People are like, 'I can't believe you're admitting that s--- in front of a whole group of people,'" Mr. O'Malley said. "And I'm like, 'Guess what? It can't hurt me anymore!'"</p><p>The show ran from 2003 to 2006 at Second City and ImprovOlympic and was also performed at the Beverley Arts Center.</p><p>A lifelong Chicagoan, Mr. O'Malley seemed destined for greatness in the late 1980s, bounding from small sketch groups to Second City's touring company and its famed mainstage on Wells Street — the springboard for some of the country's top comic actors. He waited for his turn at fame to follow.</p><p>"I just thought it was inevitable," Mr. O'Malley said in 2003. "And all I got was a Coors Light commercial."</p><p>The big breaks went to his Second City peers. Joel Murray and Bonnie Hunt landed a sitcom. Chris Farley and Tim Meadows, his co-stars on the mainstage, went to "Saturday Night Live."</p><p>Mr. O'Malley seethed, drank and snorted cocaine, the glamour drug of the era.</p><p>"At the time I thought I was fine because everybody I liked was on coke," he recalled. "Everybody I looked up to was high. It was like, 'Oh, I'm cool. It sharpens me.'"</p><p>He opened one show after another at Second City, making enemies as readily as he made people laugh. "I was a major pain in the ass," he said. "I would come to rehearsals and throw chairs and say, 'F--- you! I ain't doing one of your stupid scenes again!' "</p><p>Back then a Second City actor with enough experience or enough nerve could dominate his cast members — not to mention his director — and O'Malley figured his turn had come. "I thought I was the alpha male," he said, "and [instead] I was the big jerk drunk cokehead."</p><p>As his fifth mainstage show began to wind down in 1992, the Second City producers sat Mr. O'Malley down for a chat. "They were real kind about it. Instead of saying, 'You're drinking and you're a complete a—hole and nobody likes you anymore,' they just said, 'Don't you think it's time to move on?' And I'm like, 'Yeah.'"</p><p>A few more stage gigs came along. Then, nothing.</p><p>"It started to get really depressing," O'Malley told the Sun-Times in 2003. "I ended up, like, bartending in Beverly. I'm sitting there on Sunday night watching two guys beat the s--- out of each other over whether we should watch the hockey game or 'The Three Stooges,' going, 'What in the f--- happened to my life?' "</p><p>Before long, he was using crack. Friends begged him to clean up, but nothing sank in until his younger sister called one day. "She was just cryin' on the phone because I'd stolen money from her," he said in 2003. "And she was like, 'Tim, just don't f---in' die. Everyone thinks you're gonna die. I think you're gonna die. Please don't die.' "</p><p>Mr. O'Malley entered rehab, rediscovered religion, taught at the Second City Training Center and attended and led recovery meetings.</p><p>""Godshow' is his legacy, the best art he ever made, and a vehicle for helping people," said his life partner Pamela Staker. "When 'Godshow' was running, the whole recovery community showed up in force." </p><p>For decades, Mr. O'Malley served as a listener and guidepost for people struggling with addiction, including many in the improv and comedy scene.</p><p>"I think 'Godshow' allowed people to see that you could be in recovery and at the same time go on and be in comedy and still have your identity and your edge," said Laura Hugg, a friend and comic who is part of the recovery community.</p><p>"There is a concern that 'Oh, if I get healthy, get my act together, the talent won't be there, the ability won't be there,' and I think Tim knew and carried the message of 'You won't stop being funny if you stop doing things that are killing you,'" Hugg said.</p><p>Mr. O'Malley was born June 26, 1957, and grew up in Beverly, one of 11 children.</p><p>His death came two days after Kevin Doyle, another well known South Side Irish Catholic Second City alum.</p><p>"Tim was amazing on stage," said former Second City producer Cheryl Sloane. "If there was ever a problem and you needed somebody to hold the audience for a minute, you could send Tim out on stage."</p><p>"Audiences could relate to him, they saw themselves in him, and he was funny as can be and quick witted. He could take anybody on one-on-one in wit," she said.</p><p>At Second City, Mr. O'Malley invented a character named "Coffee Man" who crashed any scene if an actor said the word "coffee," recalled John Rubano, a former Second City castmate.</p><p>"He was a jittery coffee-drinking maniac and whether you wanted him to or not, he would appear as "Coffee man" and he'd say 'Just don't say 'coffee' and you won't get Coffee Man," Rubano said with a laugh. </p><p>Most recently Mr. O'Malley performed in a series of online ads for Mr. Submarine.</p><p>Services are pending.<br></p>

entries.title: West Englewood fire deaths ruled homicides: autopsies
entries.summary: <p>The deaths of four people — including two children — in a suspicious extra alarm West Englewood neighborhood fire have all been rules homicides, officials said Thursday afternoon.</p><p>Autopsies performed Thursday by the Cook County medical examiner's office determined they died of thermal injuries and carbon monoxide toxicity due to the fire, according to the medical examiner's office. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/20/3-kids-among-6-critically-hurt-in-suspicious-2-alarm-fire-at-west-englewood-home-sources" target="_blank" >Their deaths, including 8-year-old Royalty Ratler, were ruled a homicides. </a></p><p>The blaze erupted early Wednesday in a house in the 6200 block of South Paulina Street, and left Royalty, an unidentified 15-year-old boy, 57-year-old Lisa Brown and 57-year-old Reginald Lee Wilson dead. Two other people remain in critical condition, officials said. </p><p>Police are investigating the blaze in the 6200 block of South Paulina Street as arson.</p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for updates.</i></p>

entries.title: From O’Hare to the hospital, here’s how Chicago is preparing for Ebola
entries.summary: <p>As a major hub for international travel, Chicago is no stranger to preparing for and handling deadly contagions.</p><p>The city developed a playbook more than a decade ago during an Ebola outbreak in west Africa and is using lessons learned for the <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/05/20/nx-s1-5826910/ebola-outbreak-africa-risks" target="_blank" ><u>deadly virus</u></a> as it surges in the Democratic Republic of Congo.</p><p>Public health leaders and infectious diseases specialists are preparing for everything from where to send patients in Chicago should they develop symptoms to how to get travelers safely through uber-busy O’Hare Airport.</p><p>Here’s what you should know.</p><h3><b>First of all, there’s a low risk of Ebola arriving in Chicago. </b></h3><h3></h3><p>There are no confirmed cases of Ebola across the city, according to the Chicago public health department. A person can’t spread the virus unless they have symptoms such as nausea or diarrhea, so they aren’t as contagious. That means it’s easier to protect people compared to how COVID-19 spread rapidly through the air, said Dr. Larry Kociolek, vice president of system preparedness, prevention and response at Lurie Children’s Hospital in Chicago.</p><p>A big way Ebola could arrive is through travelers at O’Hare. But that risk has been reduced.</p><p>The U.S. Department of Homeland Security is <a class="Link" href="https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2026-10179.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>routing all flights </u></a>that include any passengers who have recently traveled to the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, or South Sudan, where the virus is surging or is nearby, to Washington Dulles International Airport in Washington D.C., for enhanced Ebola screening — not to O’Hare.</p><h3><b>Chicago routinely trains for this</b></h3><p>Ever since the 2014 Ebola outbreak led Chicago to create a plan in case a contagion arrives, public health and hospital leaders routinely meet to share intel.</p><p>Everyone from doctors to firefighters practice what to do — how to carefully draw blood from someone infected with a virus, how to put on and take off all the protective gear needed to treat a patient, and how to prepare an ambulance to safely transport someone who is sick.</p><p>It wasn’t too long ago that COVID-19 tested these skills.</p><h3><b>Still, what happens if</b> <b>someone develops Ebola symptoms? </b></h3><p>There are two designated hospitals where anyone in Illinois would receive treatment. Adults would head to Rush University Medical Center on the Near West Side, and kids and teens would go to Lurie near downtown.</p><p>Each hospital can quickly convert a large space or several patient rooms into a biocontainment unit to treat people with dangerous, highly infectious diseases.</p><p>Rush and Lurie can each treat up to two patients at a time, which doesn’t sound like a lot, but hospital leaders explained how resource intensive treating a patient with Ebola could be. For example, they need one room to treat a patient and another for nurses and doctors to change into protective gear. They need to use their own equipment for blood work — not a general hospital lab — and need specialized transport for medical waste.</p><p>Up to 50 people with the proper training could be involved in taking care of just one patient in the first 24 hours of their arrival, according to Rush.</p><p>“The stakes are much, much higher, and it is incredibly expensive to maintain those types of facilities, to maintain that equipment,” Kociolek said.</p><p>There isn’t a cure or much treatment for the swelling strain of Ebola. But doctors can provide IV fluids if a patient is dehydrated or put them on a ventilator to help them breathe, Kociolek said.</p><p>While the risk for Ebola is a little higher than it was before the outbreak, Kociolek isn’t too concerned: “For us, it's kind of just another day.”</p><p>Dr. Brian Stein, chief quality officer for the Rush University System for Health, encourages patients to still come to the hospital for emergencies or routine procedures even if they’re treating someone with Ebola: “There’s no threat to other patients.”</p><p>Both hospitals last year <a class="Link" href="https://www.rush.edu/news/rush-serve-elite-infectious-disease-center" target="_blank" ><u>received state funding</u></a> to help pay for training and equipment.</p><h3><b>Are politics getting in the way of preparedness?</b></h3><p>Public health officials in the Democratic stronghold of Illinois have been at odds with the Republican Trump administration, especially over childhood vaccines. But Dr. Emily Landon, an infectious diseases specialist at UChicago Medicine, said public health officials are working together to limit the outbreak.</p><p>“As long as we follow through with the steps that we know are going to protect individuals and communities, then I think that we’re going to be in pretty good shape,” Landon said.</p><p>Though the Trump administration <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/withdrawing-the-united-states-from-the-worldhealth-organization/" target="_blank" ><u>withdrew </u></a>from the World Health Organization, Chicago is still getting intel from WHO and from the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said Dr. Alex Sloboda, deputy commissioner of emergency preparedness and immunizations for the Chicago public health department.</p><h3><b>Should I still hop on a plane for Memorial Day weekend or summer vacation? </b></h3><p>Kociolek’s advice: “Be aware of the situation without fear. Just be mindful of infectious disease threats no matter where you travel.”</p><p>The CDC recommends against non-essential travel to the Democratic Republic of Congo, and measles is spreading in parts of the U.S. and in other countries. Travelers can look up guidance <a class="Link" href="https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/destinations/list" target="_blank" ><u>here</u></a>.</p><p><i>The Sun-Times’ Elvia Malagon contributed.</i></p><p><i>Kristen Schorsch covers the health of the region for WBEZ.</i></p>

entries.title: Police release picture of alleged East Side shooter sought in homicide
entries.summary: <p>Police are asking for the public’s help in identifying the person accused of shooting three men, one fatally, earlier this month .</p><p>A picture of that suspected gunman was released Wednesday by Chicago police, who hope someone who recognizes them will contact authorities.</p><p>One of those hit, Lisandrio Rios Ortiz, 28, died Monday night of complications from a gunshot wound to the flank, a Wednesday autopsy determined, according to the Cook County medical examiner’s office.</p><p>The gunman being sought opened fire on Ortiz and two other men on May 11 about 5:40 p.m. in the 9900 block of South Ewing Avenue, Chicago police said. That incident occurred in East Side, an area along the Indiana border near the southest edge of the city limits.</p><p>Ortiz, of the 9600 block of Avenue M, was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center. He was pronounced dead there on Monday at 9:40 p.m., according to the medical examiner’s office.</p><p>Two other men, ages 41 and 52, were shot in the abdomen. The younger man was in good condition at Advocate Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn while the 52-year-old man was listed in critical condition at the University of Chicago Medical Center, police said at the time.</p><p>No arrests have been made.</p><p>Anyone with information about the person pictured should reach out to Area 2 detectives at (312) 747-8271 or submit an anonymous tip at CPDTIP.com and use reference RD # JK250868.<br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Chicago man charged with assaulting ICE agent in Brighton Park
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago man has been charged with assaulting a federal immigration agent with his car last October in Brighton Park.</p><p>Diego Emmanuel Reyes, 21, is accused of ramming his SUV into the back of a pickup truck driven by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Oct. 4 in the 3700 block of South Kedzie Avenue.</p><p>Video of the incident shows the driver of a black SUV pushing a silver pickup truck with its emergency lights activated into a lane on Kedzie Avenue that was closed for construction.</p><p>The driver of the SUV rams the truck again and backs up, as a federal agent who exited the truck points a gun at the SUV driver, according to the video.</p><p>The SUV driver then drives through a construction traffic barrier and flees, the video shows.</p><p>The federal indictment of Reyes was returned Wednesday. It charges him with assaulting, impeding, intimidating and interfering with an ICE officer using a deadly weapon.</p><p>An arraignment in federal court has not yet been scheduled.</p><p>U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros called the alleged ramming "a dangerous and brazen act of violence against a federal agent as well as an attack on the rule of law."</p><p>"Federal agents perform risky, essential work every single day to enforce our federal laws and keep our communities safe," Boutros said in a statement. "The Chicago U.S. Attorney’s Office will never tolerate such conduct and will continue to hold accountable those who seek to assault, impede, intimidate, or interfere with lawful federal operations."</p><p>“The Chicago Field Office has zero tolerance for anyone impeding federal officers engaged in their lawful functions," added Douglas DePodesta, special agent-in-charge of the FBI Chicago field office. "The people of Chicago deserve to be safe and free from harm. The FBI is committed to using every available resource against those who undermine the rule of law and jeopardize the peace in our community.”</p><p>On the same day as this incident — and just two blocks away — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/10/04/shooting-involving-federal-agents-in-brighton-park-under-investigation" >a U.S. Customs and Border Protection agent shot Marimar Martinez</a>.</p><p>Officials have not indicated the two incidents are related. The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Federal prosecutors initially charged Martinez and another driver, Anthony Ian Santos Ruiz, with assaulting and impeding a federal agent but later <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/20/operation-midway-blitz-marimar-martinez-anthony-ruiz-us-supreme-court-feds-drop-case-against-woman-shot-by-border-patrol-agent-in-brighton-park" >dropped charges against both of them</a>.</p>

entries.title: Encuentran cuerpo de adolescente baleado y atado tras su mamá recibir una llamada sobre su secuestro
entries.summary: <p>La madre de un joven de 18 años recibió una llamada aterradora desde Venezuela: le dijeron que su hijo había sido secuestrado y le indicaron dónde encontrarlo.</p><p>La noche del martes, la policía encontró su cuerpo, según un informe del Departamento de Policía de Chicago (CPD).</p><p>La policía emitió un comunicado en el que se indica que los oficiales que respondieron a una solicitud de visita de bienestar fueron a un apartamento en la cuadra 6800 al sur de Perry Avenue a eso de las 9 p.m. del martes.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-270000" name="module-270000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Allí encontraron a Cristian José Rojas Barrios, a quien le habían disparado en el pecho y en la pierna, y que yacía boca abajo en una bañera con las manos atadas detrás de la espalda, según el informe. Se encontraron tres casquillos de bala de 9 mm cerca de su cuerpo. Fue declarado muerto en el lugar.</p><p>Según el informe de la policía, la madre de Rojas Barrios no conocía a la persona que llamó desde Venezuela. Quien llamó le dijo que su hijo había sido secuestrado a eso de las 3 p.m. el lunes cerca de una cancha de baloncesto en la cuadra 7100 al sur de King Drive y que podrían encontrarlo dentro de un apartamento en la dirección de Perry Avenue.</p><p>Una autopsia realizada el miércoles determinó que Rojas Barrios murió a causa de múltiples lesiones sufridas en un ataque y que su fallecimiento fue clasificado como homicidio, según la Oficina del Médico Forense del Condado de Cook.</p><p>Los detectives del Área 1 estaban investigando.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: NASCAR champion Kyle Busch has died at 41
entries.summary: <p>CONCORD, N.C. — Kyle Busch, a two-time Cup Series champion who won more races than anyone across NASCAR's three national series, has died. He was 41.</p><p>The Busch Family, Richard Childress Racing and NASCAR issued a joint statement Thursday saying Busch died after being hospitalized. No cause of death was given.</p><p>Busch's family said earlier Thursday that he was hospitalized with a "severe illness," three days before he was to compete in the Coca-Cola 600 at Charlotte Motor Speedway.</p><p>Busch was the younger brother of Kurt Busch, a NASCAR Hall of Famer.</p><p>"Our entire NASCAR family is heartbroken by the loss of Kyle Busch," the statement said. "A future Hall of Famer, Kyle was a rare talent, one who comes along once in a generation. He was fierce, he was passionate, he was immensely skilled and he cared deeply about the sport and fans."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">We are saddened and heartbroken to share the news of the passing of Kyle Busch, a two-time Cup champion and one of our sport's greatest and fiercest drivers. He was 41 years old.<br><br>We extend our deepest condolences to the Busch family, Richard Childress Racing and the entire… <a href="https://t.co/FARIF6OKrw">pic.twitter.com/FARIF6OKrw</a></p>— NASCAR (@NASCAR) <a href="https://twitter.com/NASCAR/status/2057577365543301405?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 21, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The statement went on to say that "throughout a career that spanned more than two decades, Kyle set records in national series wins, won championships at NASCAR's highest level and fostered the next generation of drivers as an owner in the Truck Series. His sharp wit and competitive spirit sparked a deep emotional connection with race fans of every age, creating the proud and loyal 'Rowdy Nation.'"</p><p>The news comes 11 days after Busch radioed into his crew near the end of a Cup Series race at Watkins Glen asking a doctor to give him a "shot" after he finished the race. According to the TV broadcast, Busch had been struggling with a sinus cold that was exacerbated by the intense G-forces and elevation changes at the New York road course.</p><p>Busch finished the race in eighth place.</p><p>Busch competed at Dover last weekend and won the Trucks Series race for Richard Childress Racing. He finished 17th at the NASCAR All-Star race.</p><p>"Absolute shock. Very hard to process," veteran NASCAR driver Brad Keselowski posted on social media.</p><p>NASCAR driver and former teammate Denny Hamlin posted on social media: "Absolutely cannot comprehend this news. We just need to think of his family during this time. We love you KB."</p><p>A polarizing figure known as "Rowdy" and "Wild Thing" for his post-race fights, regular feuds with other drivers and sometimes outlandish behavior, the multi-talented Busch stormed on the Cup Series scene in 2005 by winning Rookie of the Year.</p><p>He went on to win championships in 2015 and 2019 for Joe Gibbs Racing.</p><p>From Las Vegas, Busch experienced unrivaled success across NASCAR's three national series winning a combined 234 Cup, O'Reilly Auto Parts and Trucks Series races. He had 63 Cup victories along with 102 O'Reilly Auto Parts wins and 69 Trucks victories — both records.</p><p>Kyle Busch was a racing prodigy.</p><p>He was said to be ready to race at NASCAR's top level at 16, but a cigarette settlement banned his debut and he had to wait until he was a 18. At the time Kurt Busch said "if you think I'm good, wait until you see my brother."</p><p>Busch was fired early in his career by Hendrick Motorsports to make room on the team for Dale Earnhardt Jr.</p><p>"Kyle and I had a really challenging existence for many years," Earnhardt said in a statement. "But we luckily took the time to figure out our differences and that was something he instigated with a conversation in his bus around how we each managed our racing teams. I was super eager for us to get on better terms. But it was he who made the effort for that to be possible."</p><p>Busch moved on to Joe Gibbs Racing where he experienced the vast majority of career success. But Busch was let go when there was no sponsor after the 2022 season and joined RCR, where had struggled to win races.</p><p>His lack of success led to a recent spat with former JGR teammate Denny Hamlin, who appeared to criticize Busch on the Actions Detrimental podcast. Hamlin said, "If you're expecting Kyle Busch to just go back to Victory Lane on a regular basis, you are kidding yourselves."</p><p>While Hamlin later said he meant no harm by the comments and was just making an observation, Busch took exception and said he could make Hamlin's life "hell" on the racetrack.</p><p>While several laps down at last month's race at Kansas, Busch made good on the threat and raced Hamlin hard instead of allowing the race leader to pass. That decision held up Hamlin during a crucial stage of the race and Tyler Reddick wound up winning the race after Hamlin faded late.</p><p>After winning the Trucks race at Dover last week and showing an uptick in speed, Busch seemed to make a veiled jab at Hamlin, saying "I guess I just remembered how to drive."</p><p>After earning his win at Dover, Busch was asked how many races he wants to win in his career before he stops racing.</p><p>"You take whatever you can get, man," Busch said. "You never know when the last one is going to be, so cherish them all — trust me."</p><p>The unexpected death is just the latest tragedy to hit NASCAR. Last December, former driver Greg Biffle, his wife and two children and three others died in a plane crash in Statesville, North Carolina.</p><p>The announcement of Busch's death came after Indy Car teams had already left Gasoline Alley on media day at the Indianapolis 500. As word spread on Main Street in Speedway, Indiana, just a short walk from Indianapolis Motor Speedway, race fans -- IndyCar and NASCAR -- were saddened.</p><p>"Shocking, you know, wonder what got him. He had a serious illness," said Mike Bowers, an IndyCar fan who came to town from Kansas City for the big weekend. "A sad deal. It's going to be on everybody's mind all weekend."</p><p>NASCAR officials confirmed to The Associated Press the Coca-Cola 600 will go on as planned Sunday.</p><p>Drivers are expected to begin making their way to Charlotte Motorsports Speedway in Concord on Friday with practice and qualifying beginning on Saturday. Earlier in the day, RCR had announced that Austin Hill would replace Busch in the No. 8 Chevrolet Camaro ZL1.</p><p>Busch is survived by wife Samantha and children Brexton and Lennix.</p>

He was taken to Comers Children’s Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>No one is in custody.</p>

entries.title: Sky's defensive swagger is real but the element of surprise is gone
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> came into the season thinking that the league was underestimating them defensively, and so far, they’ve been right.</p><p>The team has a top-five defensive rating through five games, trailing only the Dream, Valkyries, Aces and Fever. Not bad company to keep — and not a bad turnaround from last year when they were one of the worst defensive teams in the league.</p><p>Of course it’s an entirely new roster, and the athleticism on it has allowed Coach Tyler Marsh to take a different approach.</p><p>"This year we're more on the side of being aggressive and disruptive," Marsh said. "Last year was more of a conservative approach, and containing the ball and being somewhat constrained to certain matchups.</p><p>“We just have a different type of roster and a different type of versatility that we can explore this year, and so it allows for more aggression, with our ability to impact the ball on the perimeter first and foremost, and hope that that takes some of the pressure off our [post players protecting the rim]."</p><p>The combination of ball pressure from supremely athletic guards — Skylar Diggins, Natasha Cloud, Jacy Sheldon and Gabriela Jaquez — and rim protection from the bigs has been effective and generated excitement.</p><p>Cloud couldn’t stop raving about the defense after the win in Minnesota last week.</p><p>"I've been in the league 11 years and a lot of times I'm the only primary defender on the perimeter," Cloud said. "I can't tell you what a relief it is to have [Jaquez] on the side with me, [Sheldon], [Diggins] on the wings with me. We all can defend, we can all be super versatile. We get up, we're aggressive, and it allows us to get deflections, push offenses out of where they want to be."</p><p>The first five games have made clear who the Sky (3-2) are trying to be. Tough. Connected. Bringing heavy pressure. But for a defensive-minded identity to really take root, it needs to be tested over time.</p><p>Losing forward Rickea Jackson to a season-ending ACL injury is one such test. She didn’t come into the season known for her defense, but she was already showing that her athleticism, length and instincts for the ball translated to that end, too.</p><p>The Sky will have to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/05/20/filling-jackson-hole-sky-explore-options-for-replacing-injured-star" >figure out how to make up for that.</a></p><p>Another test is how they respond to slippage. The Sky gave up 99 points in their loss to the Wings — only the second time they'd allowed more than 90 this season.</p><p>Diggins credited some incredible shotmaking from the Wings' backcourt. Arike Ogunbowale and Paige Bueckers combined for 47 points, including 9 3-pointers. But Diggins still thought it came down to their own mistakes.</p><p>"I think we're just a little bit more undisciplined than we usually are defensively... We kind of just cut corners defensively," Diggins said after the loss. "In that third quarter we didn't get a consecutive stop, and I thought that was very uncharacteristic of what our defense was looking like the first four games."</p><p>In their second win of the season, the Sky's ball pressure smothered the Valkyries, holding them to the third-lowest field goal percentage in franchise history. In their third, their pressure seriously bothered All-Star guards Courtney Williams and Kayla McBride in Minnesota.</p><p>But now those teams know. The element of surprise — or even underestimation — is gone.</p><p>The Lynx return to Wintrust Arena on Saturday. Minnesota coach Cheryl Reeve's teams are also typically disruptive defensively — which means she might know a thing or two about how to weaponize it against you.</p><p>Are the Sky ready for her response?</p><p>Their counters and adjustments will define them much more than their original game plan.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true"
